meta.tagline: The harbour where skyscrapers meet mountains, and dim sum meets neon

pills: The Star Ferry still costs pocket change

overview.title: Welcome to Hong Kong
overview.intro: Hong Kong is a harbour of contradictions, and that is exactly why it's addictive: ten minutes from the world's densest forest of skyscrapers, subtropical mountain trails begin; the double-decker tram trundles beneath neon signs while the metro runs to the second. In the morning, tai chi is practised in the shadow of a bamboo-scaffolded tower; at noon dim sum arrives in steaming baskets; at night the harbour stands to attention for a light show on both banks. This city never slows down — but it has the grace to let you catch your breath on the Star Ferry's deck.

local_word.definition: 加油 — literally 'add oil': the Hong Kong way of saying 'keep going, hang in there, you've got this!'. At the marathon, in the exam hall, on the uphill stairs — the city's spirit in two syllables.

rules.title: Don't take a step without an Octopus card
rules.description: The Octopus works everywhere — metro, tram, ferry, supermarket — and reduces your turnstile life to seconds. Buy it at the airport, top it up, forget about it — the tourist hunting for cash in this city is forever in a queue.

rules.title: Stand right on the escalator, walk fast
rules.description: Hong Kong's tempo is high: the escalator's left is for walkers, the right for standers, and nobody will explain the rule — they simply live it. Match the flow in a crowd, and step aside to check your map.

rules.title: Share the cha chaan teng table
rules.description: At busy hours being seated with strangers at a local diner (cha chaan teng) is normal: don't be surprised — nod, look at the menu. Fast ordering, fast eating, passing the table on — this is a rhythm, not rudeness.

quick_facts.label: Getting around
quick_facts.sub: The Octopus card covers them all

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: Light show every night at 8 pm

tip.label: The Hong Kong philosophy
tip.text: Explore this city vertically: markets at street level, restaurants on the middle floors, bars on the rooftops, trails on the mountain. Five different cities live at the same address — the lift buttons are your map.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Hong Kong's transport is a sightseeing programme in itself: a century-old tram, a legendary ferry and the world's most efficient metro meet on one card.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The Airport Express reaches Central in 24 minutes, with free shuttles fanning out to the big hotels. The budget alternative, buses A11/A21, is scenic and half the price.

items.title: The MTR — a backbone that runs to the second
items.description: The metro network weaves both shores and the New Territories: clean, fast, flawlessly signed. Be ready for the human tide at rush hour — the flow carries you; just steer.

items.title: The Ding Ding — the double-decker tram
items.description: The double-deckers have trundled along the island since 1904 and remain the city's cheapest tour: take the front seat on the top deck and glide beneath the neon signs. Board at the back, pay as you leave.

items.title: The Star Ferry — the harbour's legend
items.description: The green-and-white ferries have linked the two shores since 1888 and give the world's best view cruise for pocket change: the evening crossing from Kowloon, as the skyline lights up, is the stuff of legend.

items.title: The Peak Tram and the cable cars
items.description: The Peak Tram has climbed steeply to Victoria Peak since 1888; the Ngong Ping 360 cable car glides to the Big Buddha on Lantau. Both love a queue — first departures of the morning are the rule.

callout.label: Ferry tip
callout.text: Board the Star Ferry at Tsim Sha Tsui just before sunset, cross to the island and come back: the two tickets together cost less than a coffee, and this is the only 'harbour cruise' that watches the 8 pm light show from the water.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Hong Kong choosing a shore is choosing a character: the island's financial polish, Kowloon's neon energy, or the islands' calm?

local_word.definition: Hong Kong's fast local diner: milk tea, crispy toast, noodle soup and an east-west menu. A 1950s invention and the city's everyday culinary identity — a neighbourhood is measured by its cha chaan teng.

items.name: Central and Sheung Wan
items.description: Antique lanes between the finance towers, the Mid-Levels escalator and SoHo's restaurants: the island's heart. High prices, flawless location — the classic for a first visit.

items.name: Tsim Sha Tsui (Kowloon)
items.description: The skyline view from the harbour's edge: museums, the Star Ferry pier and Nathan Road's energy. Remember the skyline photo is taken from this side — your hotel window can be a gallery.

items.name: Wan Chai and Causeway Bay
items.description: Markets, the tram line, nightlife and shopping floors interlocked: the island's dense everyday life. Hotels for every budget, something open at every hour.

items.name: Mong Kok and Yau Ma Tei
items.description: Neon signs, street markets and one of the densest crowds on earth: Hong Kong unfiltered. From cheap guesthouses to boutique hotels — for those who like their reality in high doses.

items.name: Lantau and the islands
items.description: Lantau of the Big Buddha, the fishing island Cheung Chau or laid-back Lamma: another tempo half an hour by ferry. For those who want the city + nature balance built into where they sleep.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Read the subtropical calendar like this: October-December is the golden window, summer is humid and typhoon-prone, spring misty but alive.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Misty Vitality
items.subtitle: Spring · Mild days, harbour mist
items.description: The air warms, the humidity slowly climbs, and on some mornings the harbour wraps itself in mist — the Peak view becomes a lottery. The art season floods the city with galleries in spring.

callout.label: March tip
callout.text: In late March the art weeks take over: giant fairs, museum nights and rooftop events. Check the webcam before heading up the Peak — if it's misty, swap the programme; the art is always open.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Humidity and Typhoon Season
items.subtitle: Summer · 90% humidity, air-conditioned refuges
items.description: The heat and humidity are heavy and the occasional typhoon signal stops the city; but hotels get cheaper, and the malls and museums are icy cool. Island beaches and junk-boat days are this season's reward.

callout.label: Typhoon note
callout.text: If the typhoon signal reaches 8, the city officially stops: ferries and cable cars close, shutters come down. Track the signal in the app and turn that day into a museum-and-food day — the city reopens a day later as if nothing happened.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Golden Window
items.subtitle: Autumn · Clear skies, trail season
items.description: Humidity drops, the sky clears and the city returns to its best self: the Peak view sharp, the trails cool, the terraces full. This is the year's most reliable travel window — everyone knows it, so book early.

callout.label: November tip
callout.text: In November walk the Dragon's Back: an ocean-view ridge hike minutes from the city, ending with a swim at Shek O beach. The 'skyscraper city' prejudice breaks on this trail.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Cool and Festive
items.subtitle: Winter · Mild cool, New Year fever
items.description: Winter is gentle — cardigan weather, not coat weather. In late January-February the Chinese New Year paints the city red: flower markets, the night parade and fireworks over the harbour. Some businesses close for a few festival days.

callout.label: New Year tip
callout.text: If you're here for Chinese New Year, hit the Victoria Park flower market on the eve and watch the second night's fireworks from the Kowloon waterfront. Book the hotel early — the whole region has the same idea.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Hong Kong holds some of the densest delicious square metres on earth: Michelin-starred dim sum and back-alley wonton live in the same block.

local_word.definition: 飲茶 — 'to drink tea': but its real meaning is a long dim sum table with friends. The baskets arrive in waves, and when the teapot runs dry you leave the lid ajar — the silent language for 'more tea, please'.

items.name: Dim sum — a ritual by the basket
items.description: Har gow (shrimp dumplings), siu mai, char siu bao: the table builds itself as the steaming baskets land. A morning-and-noon ritual — dim sum without tea is dim sum incomplete.

items.name: Char siu and roast goose
items.description: The glossy red char siu and crisp-skinned roast goose hanging in the windows: the shopfront pride of Cantonese cooking. A portion over rice is the city's best fast meal.

items.name: Wonton noodles and fish balls
items.description: Shrimp-filled wontons over fine egg noodles: the century-old speciality of tiny shops. The street stall's fish-ball soup plays in the same league.
items.tag: In a tiny shop · being squeezed in is good luck

items.name: Cha chaan teng classics
items.description: Silk-stocking milk tea, a pineapple bun (bolo bao) with a slab of cold butter, and Hong Kong-style French toast: the warmest menu of the east-west mix. Afternoon tea is drunk here.

items.name: Egg tarts and egg waffles
items.description: A warm egg tart (dan tat) from the oven and the bubble-textured egg waffle (gai daan jai): the city's two sweet signatures. Whichever bakery has the queue is the right bakery.
items.tag: Street sweet · warm from the oven

items.name: A dai pai dong evening
items.description: Wok flames at open-air stalls, plastic stools and ice-cold beer: the smoky flavour called 'wok hei' (the breath of the wok) is born here. Their numbers have dwindled — when you find one, don't pass it by.
items.tag: At an open stall · by wok fire

callout.label: The table rule
callout.text: Fill your neighbour's cup before your own, and accept thanks by two fingers tapped lightly on the table — this silent courtesy is the table's heart. Don't fear the menu-less place: point + show how many you are; that method never leaves you hungry in this city.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone goes up the Peak; these six open Hong Kong's layers.

items.name: The Lugard Road walk
items.description: Five minutes from the Peak Tram terrace's crowds, a flat path circles the summit: the skyline at your feet, no queue, no entry fee. The sunset loop takes 45 minutes — the city's best free view.

items.name: Man Mo Temple
items.description: A dim temple in the middle of Sheung Wan with giant incense coils hanging from the ceiling, dedicated to the gods of literature and war. At the foot of the skyscrapers, you step into another century in an instant.

items.name: The Temple Street night market
items.description: As evening falls the stalls, fortune tellers and open-air karaoke booths appear: the set of Hong Kong cinema in real life. Haggling allowed, atmosphere free.

items.rarity: A thousand lives in one building
items.name: Yick Fat / Montane Mansion
items.description: Quarry Bay's colossal housing blocks are famous as the 'monster building': look up from the courtyard and the city's density explains itself in one frame. With respect and quiet for the residents — this is a home, not a film set.

items.name: Cheung Chau island
items.description: A car-free fishing island 40 minutes by ferry: the smell of dried fish, bicycles, mini beaches and a pirate's cave. The locals' Sunday escape — go on a weekday and find it empty.

items.rarity: Tai chi at dawn on the waterfront
items.name: Sunrise on the Kowloon promenade
items.description: The Tsim Sha Tsui promenade at 6 am: the skyline turns pink, locals practise tai chi, runners pass. Choose this quiet hour over the light show crowds — the harbour saves its most beautiful face for morning.

callout.label: Trail tip
callout.text: Most of Hong Kong's land is mountain and park: give half a day to Dragon's Back, Lion Rock or a Lantau trail. From a summit you understand — this is not a skyscraper city, it's a nature reserve with skyscrapers.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Hong Kong is honest and orderly; its traps are few but well camouflaged along the tourist route.

items.name: The midday Peak Tram queue
items.description: At midday the tram queue reaches an hour; on a misty day you meet a white wall at the top — ticket paid, view a lottery.
items.instead: Take the first tram of the morning or climb by bus 15 on the winding road; at the top, walk Lugard Road's free view instead of the paid Sky Terrace. If it's misty, swap the day.

items.name: The Nathan Road electronics shops
items.description: Some electronics and camera shops on the tourist strip inflate the price afterwards, swap the box or play the 'mandatory accessory' game.
items.instead: Buy electronics from chain stores or official dealers, and verify prices online. Never enter a shop without price tags in the window.

items.name: The surprise bill at a view restaurant
items.description: Some harbour-view tourist restaurants pad the bill with service, tea and 'peanut' line items; the menu price is half the story.
items.instead: Treat the tea-and-snack charge as normal (it's local custom) but know the rates: 10% service + a small tea charge is standard. Take the view with one drink at a bar, eat at a local place.

items.name: Insisting on a taxi for a short hop
items.description: In traffic hours a taxi is both dearer and slower; the MTR often does the same route in half the time.
items.instead: Use the MTR + tram + ferry trio with your Octopus; if you need a taxi, make sure the red (urban) cab runs its meter — there is no haggling taxi in this city.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Queue culture in Hong Kong is sacred and well signposted: smile politely at anyone offering a queue-free 'shortcut' and walk on. The city's system works with the same efficiency for visitors — trust the system.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: A full loop of the vertical city, from Peak to neon

steps.title: A Peak morning
steps.description: First Peak Tram up to Victoria Peak: walk Lugard Road and see the skyline in morning light, queue-free.

steps.title: Sheung Wan and Man Mo
steps.description: The incense-coiled temple, the antique lanes and the city's layers on the Mid-Levels escalator; a side-street coffee break.

steps.title: A yum cha noon
steps.description: The dim sum table: har gow, siu mai, char siu bao and strong tea. Don't forget the two-finger thank-you as the baskets empty.

steps.title: The Ding Ding tour
steps.description: The Wan Chai-Causeway Bay stretch from the tram's top front seat: neon signs, markets and city life right outside the glass.

steps.title: Across by Star Ferry
steps.description: Cross to Kowloon towards sunset: take your place on the promenade as the skyline lights come on.

steps.title: The light show + the night market
steps.description: Watch the 8 pm Symphony of Lights from the harbour, then dive into Temple Street: stalls, fortune tellers and late-night snacks — a close beneath the neon.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Island, Kowloon and mountain — three Hong Kongs

steps.title: Classic Hong Kong
steps.description: The one-day flow above: Peak, temple, dim sum, tram, ferry, light show.

steps.title: Lantau and the Buddha
steps.description: The Ngong Ping 360 cable car to the great Tian Tan Buddha; the stilt houses of the Tai O fishing village in the afternoon; a comfortable cha chaan teng dinner on return.

steps.title: Trail and island escape
steps.description: The Dragon's Back hike + a swim at Shek O in the morning; the Cheung Chau or Lamma ferry in the afternoon; farewell at a dai pai dong with wok fire and cold beer.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: English works everywhere, but five words of Cantonese open a wide smile on the counter's far side.

items.meaning: Hello — the morning version 'jou san' is even more charming
Thanks / excuse me / may I — the magic word you'll use fifty times a day
Thank you (for a gift or big favour) — m̀h'gōi's formal sibling
'Keep going, you've got this!' — on the hill, in the queue, in life
'Delicious' — said after the dim sum basket, it wins you the counter
